# My Project

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.2.0

## Linked-Intent Development (MANDATORY)

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill for all code changes.

# High-Level Design: Note-taking App

## Problem

Users need a low-friction way to capture thoughts across devices.

## Approach

A local-first note store with cloud sync. Notes are plain text files; sync is a background reconciliation over an append-only event log.

## Target Users

Individual knowledge workers on mobile and desktop.

## Architecture

Client-side store, event-log sync server, resolver service for conflicts.

## Key Design Decisions

Local-first over cloud-first: users work offline, conflicts reconcile on reconnect.

## Goals

Low latency capture. Offline by default. No vendor lock-in on note format.

## Non-Goals

Real-time collaborative editing. Rich media beyond plain text.

# LLD: Note Store

## Context

The note store is the local persistence layer for plain-text notes. It supports create, read, update, delete, and list operations, with an event log recording every mutation.

## Architecture

Flat directory of one file per note, indexed by a SQLite database for fast listing and search.

## Behaviors

Note creation writes the file and appends a create event. Note deletion removes the file and appends a delete event. The event log is append-only; compaction is out of scope for v1.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Filesystem + SQLite | Simple, grep-friendly, survives across app upgrades. |
| Event log | Append-only JSONL | Simplest durable log; no schema evolution needed v1. |

# Note Store specs

**LLD**: docs/llds/note-store.md

## Creation

- `[x]` **NOTE-STORE-001**: When the user creates a note, the system SHALL write the note file to the notes directory and append a create event to the event log.
- `[x]` **NOTE-STORE-002**: When the user deletes a note, the system SHALL remove the note file and append a delete event to the event log.

## LID

- Version: 1.2.0

## Linked-Intent Development

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill.

# High-Level Design: Task Queue

## Problem

Background jobs must run reliably without blocking request handlers.

## Approach

A durable queue backed by Postgres; workers poll and process jobs with at-least-once delivery.

## Architecture

Producer API, jobs table, worker pool, dead-letter table.

## Tenets

- **Boring over clever.** Prefer well-worn solutions to novel ones unless the novel one is decisively better — a future maintainer should not have to reverse-engineer ingenuity.
- **When a job fails three times, move it to the dead-letter table and stop retrying.**

## Key Design Decisions

At-least-once over exactly-once: simpler, and consumers are idempotent.

## Goals

Reliable delivery. Observable failures. No lost jobs.

The recommended action is to route that entry to EARS as a spec (move it out of ## Tenets into a spec/LLD), not to keep or merely reword it as a tenet
The report does NOT flag the 'Boring over clever' entry as spec-shaped — it is a genuine class-level lean with a defensible opposite, so the coach distinguishes a real tenet from the triggered rule
The tenet finding cites the tenet-quality principle by name, paired with a plain-English gloss inline

# High-Level Design: Task Scheduler

## Problem

Scheduled and event-driven tasks must run reliably across a worker fleet.

## Approach

A durable task table polled by stateless workers; failures retried with backoff.

## Architecture

Scheduler, task table, worker pool, dead-letter queue.

## Tenets

- **Boring over clever.** Prefer well-worn solutions to novel ones unless the novel one is decisively better.
- **Correctness over speed.** When the two conflict, lean toward the slower, correct behavior.
- **Retry a failed task up to three times, then move it to the dead-letter queue.**

## Key Design Decisions

At-least-once delivery with idempotent workers.

## Goals

Reliable execution. Visible failures.

# High-Level Design: Field Notes

## Problem

Field technicians capture notes on devices that are frequently offline; notes must reconcile when connectivity returns.

## Approach

Local-first note store per device with background sync to a central service on reconnect.

## Architecture

Device-local store, sync service, reconciliation on the sync path.

## Tenets

- **Boring over clever.** Prefer well-worn solutions to novel ones unless the novel one is decisively better.

## Goals

No blocked capture in the field. Convergent state after reconnect.

## Non-Goals

Real-time collaborative editing.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: SYNC
---
# LLD: Sync

## Context

Reconciliation of device-local note edits with the central service after offline periods. Field devices' clocks are frequently wrong by several minutes; they resync NTP only when connectivity returns.

## Architecture

Each device uploads its pending edits on reconnect; the sync service merges them into the canonical store.

## Conflict handling

When two devices edited the same note while offline, the edit with the later device wall-clock timestamp wins; the losing edit is discarded.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Conflict resolution | Last-writer-wins by device wall-clock | Simpler. |
| Note storage | SQLite on device | Standard embedded store. |

# sync specs

**LLD**: docs/intent/sync/sync-design.md

- `[x]` **SYNC-001**: When a device reconnects after an offline period, the system SHALL upload its pending edits to the sync service.
- `[x]` **SYNC-002**: When two devices edited the same note while offline, the system SHALL keep the edit with the later device wall-clock timestamp and discard the other.

assertions.text: The report carries a decision-capture finding on the conflict-resolution choice as its own entry — the tradeoffs behind last-writer-wins by device wall-clock survive only as the compressed row 'Simpler.', which a cold reader cannot reconstruct — citing the decision-capture dimension or the *docs carry current intent* principle, and this finding appears ALONGSIDE any design-defect or coherence finding about clock unreliability rather than being absorbed into it

Wherever the report states a remedy for the under-captured decision (inventory line, detail section, or recommendations), it defaults to expanding the Decisions-table row — naming the rejected alternative and the accepted cost — rather than leading with 'write a decision doc'; a report that states no remedy passes provided no finding leads with a decision-doc recommendation (the coach's one-line inventory format legitimately defers actions)

If the report suggests a decision doc at all, the suggestion is justified against the reserve bar — researched options weighed against criteria at a resolution a future reader could re-run, deep work whose memory shapes the intent of the rest of the system — and not offered as the default remedy or on the grounds that the choice is contested (no doc suggestion passes vacuously)

The 'SQLite on device' storage row is NOT flagged on decision-capture grounds — no under-captured-decision finding names it (findings about it on other grounds do not fail this) — so the coach distinguishes a still-live decision from a settled-obvious one

# printfarm

Queue and dispatch service for the makerspace's shared 3D-printer farm.

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

## Navigation

| What you need | Where to look |
|---|---|
| High-level design | docs/high-level-design.md |
| Design nodes and EARS specs | docs/intent/ |

# printfarm — High-Level Design

## Problem

The makerspace runs six 3D printers shared by roughly 120 members. Today members claim printers over a chat channel, walk a USB stick to the machine, and hover until the print starts. Prints collide, long jobs monopolize the popular machines, and nobody can see what is queued. Members want to upload a sliced job from home in the evening and collect the part the next day.

## Approach

A single service on the workshop mini-PC accepts sliced G-code uploads, holds a queue per printer class, and dispatches jobs to printers over their local network APIs. Members interact through a small web UI; staff see the same queue with reordering rights.

## Architecture

Two design nodes:

- **job-queue** (`docs/intent/job-queue/`) — accepts uploads, orders jobs, dispatches to idle printers.
- **printer-registry** (`docs/intent/printer-registry/`) — knows which printers exist, their classes, and whether they are reachable and idle.

## Tenets

- A submitted job is a promise: members should be able to upload and walk away.
- Staff override members, but the queue explains itself — no silent reordering.
- The mini-PC is modest hardware; the service stays small.

## Goals

- Evening upload, overnight print, morning pickup — with no member present.
- Fair access to the popular printer classes.

## Non-Goals

- Slicing (members upload ready G-code).
- Filament inventory and billing.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: QUEUE
---

# job-queue — Design

## Context

Members upload sliced G-code from home, mostly in the evening; jobs dispatch overnight as printers free up. The service runs on the workshop mini-PC, which takes unattended OS updates and the occasional power blip. Staff reorder the queue from the same UI members use.

## Architecture

The queue is a per-printer-class list of accepted jobs held entirely in process memory. On startup the service rebuilds its picture of the farm by polling each registered printer for the job it is currently running; jobs that were accepted but not yet dispatched before a restart are gone, and members resubmit them. Uploaded G-code files are kept on disk under a content hash, so resubmitting the same file is cheap.

Dispatch is event-driven: when the registry reports a printer idle, the head job of that printer's class is sent to it.

## Dispatch behavior

- A job is accepted only if its target class has at least one registered printer.
- On dispatch failure (printer rejects or times out), the job returns to the head of its class queue and the printer is marked suspect.

## Prioritization

Two priority classes: staff and member. Within a class, first-in-first-out.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduling order | FIFO within two priority classes | Shortest-job-first rejected: members game it by splitting prints; accepted cost: one long job can hold a class for hours, mitigated by staff reordering |
| Job identifiers | Short base32 slugs | UUIDs rejected: unreadable on printer LCDs and in chat; accepted cost: slugs recycle after 90 days |
| Upload size limit | 64 MB per G-code file | Covers the largest bed at 0.1 mm layers; keeps the mini-PC disk safe |

**LLD**: docs/intent/job-queue/job-queue-design.md

- `[x]` **QUEUE-001**: When a member uploads a G-code file larger than 64 MB, the system SHALL reject the upload and state the limit.
- `[x]` **QUEUE-002**: When the registry reports a printer idle, the system SHALL dispatch the head job of that printer's class to it.
- `[x]` **QUEUE-003**: When a dispatch attempt fails, the system SHALL return the job to the head of its class queue and mark the printer suspect.
- `[x]` **QUEUE-004**: When the service starts, the system SHALL rebuild farm state by polling each registered printer for its current job.
- `[x]` **QUEUE-005**: When a staff member reorders the queue, the system SHALL record the reordering visibly in the queue view.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: REG
---

# printer-registry — Design

## Context

Six printers today across three hardware models, occasionally offline for maintenance. Staff register and retire printers; the queue asks the registry which printers are idle.

## Architecture

A registry table of printers (id, class, network address, state) persisted in a single SQLite file. State is derived from heartbeats: the registry polls each printer's status endpoint on an interval.

## Heartbeat behavior

- A printer missing three consecutive heartbeats is marked unreachable and receives no dispatches until it responds again.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Heartbeat interval | 15 s | Fast enough that idle printers pick up work promptly; slow enough not to bother printer firmware |
| Registry store | Single SQLite file | Fits the mini-PC; nothing else needs concurrent writers |

**LLD**: docs/intent/printer-registry/printer-registry-design.md

- `[x]` **REG-001**: When a printer misses three consecutive heartbeats, the system SHALL mark it unreachable and exclude it from dispatch.
- `[x]` **REG-002**: When an unreachable printer responds to a heartbeat, the system SHALL mark it idle or busy per its reported state.
- `[x]` **REG-003**: When staff retire a printer, the system SHALL stop heartbeats to it and remove it from dispatch eligibility.

assertions.text: The findings inventory contains an under-captured-decision finding, citing the *decision capture* dimension or the *docs carry current intent* principle, for the job-queue's in-memory / non-persistent queue (jobs accepted but not yet dispatched are lost when the service restarts). The finding is raised even though no file records any debate or contest over the choice — the report may not excuse or downgrade it on the grounds that the decision was never contested, since the requirement judges forward from the landed state.

The decision-capture finding for the in-memory queue stands as its own entry in the findings inventory. If the report also critiques the same choice as technically unsound or as incoherent with the HLD tenet 'a submitted job is a promise' / the overnight-print goal, that critique appears in addition to — not instead of — the capture finding. A report whose only entry about the in-memory queue is a design or coherence critique fails this assertion.

The remedy recommended for the in-memory-queue finding is the smallest sufficient capture: adding an expanded Decisions & Alternatives row in docs/intent/job-queue/job-queue-design.md that names the rejected alternative (some form of persisted or durable queue store) and the accepted cost (queued-but-undispatched jobs lost on restart, members resubmit). The report does NOT recommend a standalone decision doc for this choice.

The report does not flag any of the existing Decisions-table rows — scheduling order, job identifiers, upload size limit, heartbeat interval, registry store — as under-captured decisions, and recommends no capture remedy for any of them.

The report raises a finding that the job-queue's in-memory queue (accepted-but-undispatched jobs lost on a restart) works against the HLD tenet 'a submitted job is a promise' (or the overnight / upload-and-walk-away goal), naming the tenet or goal, the mechanism, and the restart condition. A finding that only notes the missing Decisions row, or treats it as a generic reliability concern without the tenet, does not pass.

# ledgerette

Append-only bookkeeping for freelancers and small studios.

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

## Navigation

| What you need | Where to look |
|---|---|
| High-level design | docs/high-level-design.md |
| Design nodes and EARS specs | docs/intent/ |

# ledgerette — High-Level Design

## Problem

Freelancers and two-to-five-person studios track invoices and payments in spreadsheets, then spend days each year reconstructing what happened for their accountant. Rows get edited in place, history is lost, and the accountant's first question — "what did this number look like before you fixed it?" — has no answer.

## Approach

A small ledger application in which every business event is appended to a journal and nothing is ever edited. Screens and reports are read-models derived from the journal. Mistakes are corrected by appending compensating entries, so the audit trail is the data rather than a bolt-on.

## Architecture

Three design nodes:

- **journal** (`docs/intent/journal/`) — the append-only event journal, sole source of truth.
- **reporting** (`docs/intent/reporting/`) — balances, aging, and exports derived from the journal.
- **corrections** (`docs/intent/corrections/`) — how mistakes are fixed without edits.

## Tenets

- The books are never edited, only appended.
- Every number on screen can be traced to journal lines.
- The accountant's export is a first-class product, not an afterthought.

## Goals

- A studio hands its accountant one export and answers zero follow-up questions about history.
- Any past month's report is reproducible bit-for-bit.

## Non-Goals

- Payroll, tax filing, bank integrations.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: JRNL
---

# journal — Design

## Context

The journal is the system of record. Everything else in ledgerette — balances, reports, the correction flow — is defined in terms of it.

## Architecture

An append-only journal of business events: InvoiceIssued, PaymentRecorded, CreditNoteIssued, EntryReversed. Events are serialized one per line and grouped into monthly files matching accounting periods. No event is ever modified or deleted; the corrections node defines how mistakes are handled by appending.

Read models (balances, aging) are projections rebuilt from the journal; no stored projection is authoritative.

## Append behavior

- Events carry the id of the acting user and, where they amend the meaning of an earlier event, the id of that event.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Storage model | Append-only event journal | Auditability |
| Event serialization | JSON Lines | Greppable, one event per line, tool-friendly |
| Journal file rotation | Monthly files | Matches accounting periods |

**LLD**: docs/intent/journal/journal-design.md

- `[x]` **JRNL-001**: When a business event is recorded, the system SHALL append it to the current monthly journal file and SHALL NOT modify any existing event.
- `[x]` **JRNL-002**: When an event amends the meaning of an earlier event, the system SHALL record the earlier event's id on the new event.
- `[x]` **JRNL-003**: When a projection is requested for a period, the system SHALL derive it from journal events alone.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: RPT
---

# reporting — Design

## Context

Balances, an aging report, and the accountant export. Because the journal is append-only and the sole source of truth, every report is a projection rebuilt from journal events; reproducing last March's report means replaying last March's events.

## Architecture

Projections are computed at read time and cached; the cache is disposable. The accountant export is a period's journal slice plus the derived statements.

## Report behavior

- The aging report buckets unpaid invoices by days outstanding from issue date.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Currency handling | Amounts shown in the invoice's original currency only | Simplicity |
| Report date basis | Issue date (accrual view) | Cash-basis view rejected for v1: target studios invoice on terms and think in accrual; accepted cost: unpaid invoices inflate the revenue view, mitigated by the aging report beside it |
| Export date format | ISO 8601 | The team debated this at length across two sessions; ISO 8601 won over locale-dependent formats |

**LLD**: docs/intent/reporting/reporting-design.md

- `[x]` **RPT-001**: When a balance or aging report is requested, the system SHALL rebuild it from journal events, treating any cache as disposable.
- `[x]` **RPT-002**: When the aging report is rendered, the system SHALL bucket unpaid invoices by days outstanding from issue date.
- `[x]` **RPT-003**: When an accountant export is requested for a period, the system SHALL include that period's journal slice alongside the derived statements.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: CORR
---

# corrections — Design

## Context

Users mis-key amounts and issue invoices to the wrong client. Because journal entries are immutable, a mistake is never edited away; it is corrected on the record.

## Architecture

A correction appends an EntryReversed event referencing the original, followed by the corrected event. Ledger views show reversed pairs struck through rather than hiding them, so the trail the accountant sees matches the journal.

## Correction behavior

- Reversing an already-reversed event is rejected.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Correction mechanism | Compensating entries referencing the original | In-place edit is ruled out by the journal's append-only storage model; the compensating pair keeps the audit trail whole |
| Reversal visibility | Reversed pairs shown struck through in ledger views | Hiding them rejected: accountants in interviews asked to see corrections; accepted cost: busier ledger screens |

**LLD**: docs/intent/corrections/corrections-design.md

- `[x]` **CORR-001**: When a user corrects an entry, the system SHALL append an EntryReversed event referencing the original, followed by the corrected event.
- `[x]` **CORR-002**: When a reversal targets an already-reversed event, the system SHALL reject it.
- `[x]` **CORR-003**: When a ledger view contains reversed pairs, the system SHALL show them struck through rather than hiding them.

For the reporting node's currency-handling decision (original invoice currency only, rationale 'Simplicity'), the report recommends an expanded Decisions-table row naming the rejected alternative (e.g. currency conversion at report time) and the accepted cost (e.g. no cross-currency totals) — and does NOT recommend a decision doc for this decision.

The report does NOT recommend a decision doc for the export-date-format decision, even though its row records that the team debated it at length across two sessions — a debate having occurred is not, by itself, grounds for a doc. The report also does not flag this row as under-captured: the rejected alternative (locale-dependent formats) is already named and a cold reader would not question ISO 8601.

The report does not flag the settled or already-adequate rows — event serialization (JSON Lines), journal file rotation (monthly), report date basis (issue date), correction mechanism (compensating entries), reversal visibility (struck-through pairs) — as under-captured decisions.

# shiftly

Weekly shift scheduling, swaps, and reminders for small cafe and retail teams.

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

## Navigation

| What you need | Where to look |
|---|---|
| High-level design | docs/high-level-design.md |
| Design nodes and EARS specs | docs/intent/ |

# shiftly — High-Level Design

## Problem

Small cafe and retail teams build weekly schedules in spreadsheets and trade shifts over group chat. Managers learn about a broken swap when a shift starts uncovered, and staff learn about schedule changes by scrolling.

## Approach

A small web app: managers generate and publish a weekly schedule, staff request swaps that managers approve, and everyone is told about the things that concern them by text message.

## Architecture

Three design nodes:

- **schedule-engine** (`docs/intent/schedule-engine/`) — builds the weekly draft and publishes the schedule of record.
- **swap-requests** (`docs/intent/swap-requests/`) — post-publication shift trades with approval.
- **notifications** (`docs/intent/notifications/`) — outbound messages for publications, swaps, and reminders.

## Tenets

- The published schedule is a commitment; changes after publication are explicit and visible.
- The tool never staffs a shift no manager approved.
- Staff hear about exactly the things that affect them, and nothing else.

## Goals

- A manager publishes next week's schedule in under half an hour.
- No shift starts uncovered because a swap silently fell through.

## Non-Goals

- Payroll, time clocks, demand forecasting.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: SCHED
---

# schedule-engine — Design

## Context

A manager builds next week's schedule from staff availability and per-shift role requirements, touches it up by hand, and publishes it. The design was piloted in three cafes for two months.

## Architecture

Greedy assignment fills shifts from availability in seniority order, then hands the manager an editable draft with unfilled slots highlighted. Publication freezes the draft into the schedule of record.

## Assignment behavior

- A draft cannot publish while any shift lacks a required role.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduling window | One week, published Thursday for the week starting Monday | Matches how all three pilot cafes already plan |
| Solver approach | Greedy assignment plus manual touch-up | Constraint solver rejected: in the pilot spike its infeasibility failures were opaque and managers stopped trusting the draft; accepted cost: managers hand-resolve two to three leftover conflicts a week |
| Overtime handling | Hard block at 40 hours/week | Soft warning rejected: pilot managers overrode it routinely and the compliance risk landed on the owner; accepted cost: legitimate holiday-week exceptions need an owner override |
| Shift granularity | 30-minute increments | 15-minute grain rejected: cluttered the grid without changing staffing decisions; accepted cost: staggered 15-minute starts are unsupported |

**LLD**: docs/intent/schedule-engine/schedule-engine-design.md

- `[x]` **SCHED-001**: When a draft schedule is generated, the system SHALL fill shifts greedily from availability in seniority order and highlight unfilled slots.
- `[x]` **SCHED-002**: When an assignment would put an employee over 40 hours in a week, the system SHALL block it absent an owner override.
- `[x]` **SCHED-003**: When any shift lacks a required role, the system SHALL refuse to publish the draft.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: SWAP
---

# swap-requests — Design

## Context

After publication, staff trade shifts. The published schedule is a commitment, so every change is explicit, approved, and visible.

## Architecture

A swap request names the shift and the proposed taker; the taker accepts, then a manager approves. On approval the schedule of record updates and both parties plus the manager see the change.

## Swap behavior

- A request that reaches its deadline unapproved expires, and the original assignment stands.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Approval flow | Manager approves every swap | Peer-only swaps rejected: skills coverage broke twice in the pilot; accepted cost: median four-hour swap latency |
| Eligibility | Same-role employees only | Cross-role swaps rejected: role-certification checks are out of scope for v1; accepted cost: fewer eligible takers per request |
| Swap deadline | Two hours before shift start | Leaves the manager time to re-staff if the swap falls through |

**LLD**: docs/intent/swap-requests/swap-requests-design.md

- `[x]` **SWAP-001**: When a proposed taker accepts a swap request, the system SHALL hold the schedule unchanged until a manager approves.
- `[x]` **SWAP-002**: When a manager approves a swap, the system SHALL update the schedule of record and notify both parties and the manager.
- `[x]` **SWAP-003**: When a swap request reaches two hours before shift start without approval, the system SHALL expire it and keep the original assignment.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: NOTIF
---

# notifications — Design

## Context

Staff miss schedule emails; the pilot moved to text messages and no-shows dropped.

## Architecture

Outbound messages go through an SMS gateway; each message links back to the schedule view. Publications, approved swaps, and shift reminders generate messages.

## Delivery behavior

- Messages queued during quiet hours send at the end of quiet hours.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Channel | SMS through a gateway provider | Email rejected: pilot staff missed schedule emails for days; accepted cost: per-message fees |
| Quiet hours | No messages 21:00–07:00 local | Staff asked for it in the pilot survey |
| Reminder timing | 12 hours before shift start | Matched the strongest pilot survey preference |
| Delivery retries | Three attempts over 15 minutes, then marked undelivered in the manager view | Silent failure rejected: an unaware manager is the worst outcome; accepted cost: occasional false alarms from slow carriers |

**LLD**: docs/intent/notifications/notifications-design.md

- `[x]` **NOTIF-001**: When a schedule is published, the system SHALL message each staff member their own shifts with a link to the schedule view.
- `[x]` **NOTIF-002**: When a message would send during quiet hours (21:00–07:00 local), the system SHALL queue it and send it at the end of quiet hours.
- `[x]` **NOTIF-003**: When a message fails three delivery attempts over 15 minutes, the system SHALL mark it undelivered in the manager view.

assertions.text: The report flags no decision anywhere in the project as under-captured: the findings inventory contains no decision-capture finding for any node (schedule-engine, swap-requests, notifications).

Choices a cold reader might question — greedy assignment over a constraint solver, manager approval on every swap, the hard 40-hour overtime block, SMS over email — are not flagged and draw no capture remedy, because their rows already name the rejected alternative and the accepted cost at reconstructable depth.

The report recommends no decision doc anywhere — neither for any individual decision nor as a consolidation or promotion of existing Decisions-table rows — and does not treat the pilot spikes, pilot failures, and surveys referenced in row rationales (the constraint-solver spike, the peer-swap breakage, the quiet-hours survey) as grounds for one.

The report does not recommend rewriting or expanding any of the eleven existing Decisions & Alternatives rows — including the terse ones (scheduling window, swap deadline, quiet hours, reminder timing), which cover choices a cold reader would not question.
No project files are created or modified

Doc-worthiness needs real deep work a small fixture can't hold, and forcing the recommendation on toy projects would work against doc rarity. A2 checks only that the option is named (LID-COACH-062). The authoring-time check (does the core workflow offer the doc during an options debate) is tracked separately.

# Tidewater

Leak-detection platform for a municipal water utility. Acoustic sensors clamped to distribution mains upload readings; Tidewater scores leak candidates and turns them into crew work orders.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

Consult the linked-intent-dev skill for all code changes. Design docs live in `docs/intent/`; EARS specs sit beside each design doc.

# Tidewater — High-Level Design

## Problem

The utility loses roughly 18% of treated water to leaks in its distribution mains. Most leaks are found only when they surface. About 1,400 battery-powered acoustic sensors are clamped to mains across three pressure districts; each records a noise-level and frequency-band summary every 5 minutes and uploads its buffered readings over cellular every 4 hours to conserve battery.

## Approach

Tidewater ingests sensor uploads, scores leak candidates per pipe segment, and hands confirmed-worthy candidates to the dispatch desk as crew work orders. Leak candidates are scored by an hourly batch pass over a rolling 72-hour window of readings rather than per reading as uploads arrive. Every reading, candidate, and work order is located by the utility's GIS pipe-segment ID.

## Architecture

- **sensor-ingest** — receives uploads, validates, stores raw readings.
- **leak-scoring** — the hourly scoring pass; produces leak candidates with a confidence score.
- **dispatch** — candidate queue for the dispatch desk, alerting, and work-order creation.

All three run as services against one PostgreSQL database. Staff authenticate through the utility's SSO.

## Tenets

- Crew hours are the scarce resource — a false dispatch costs more than a few hours of detection delay.
- The GIS is the system of record for where things are.
- Keep raw readings; derived data can always be recomputed.

## Goals

- Surface non-surfacing leaks before they surface.
- Keep false-dispatch rate under 15% of work orders.
- Give dispatchers a single ranked queue each morning.

## Non-Goals

- Pressure management or valve control.
- Customer-side (post-meter) leak detection.
- Sensor firmware or hardware management.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: INGEST
---

# Sensor Ingest

## Context

Sensors upload a buffered batch of 5-minute readings every 4 hours. Uploads from a district arrive staggered, and a sensor with weak signal may upload late or twice.

## Architecture

An HTTPS endpoint accepts upload batches, validates each reading against the sensor registry, and writes raw readings to the `readings` table keyed by sensor, GIS pipe-segment ID, and reading timestamp.

## Validation

Readings from unregistered sensors are rejected. Duplicate readings (same sensor, same timestamp) are dropped silently so re-uploads are harmless.

## Retention

Raw readings are retained for 72 hours in the hot `readings` table so that each hourly scoring pass can recompute candidates over the full window, including readings that arrived late. After 72 hours readings move to cold storage.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Timestamps | UTC throughout | Standard; avoids DST ambiguity |
| Duplicate handling | Drop silently on (sensor, timestamp) | Re-uploads are expected and harmless |
| Hot retention | 72 hours | Matches the scoring window |

# Sensor Ingest — EARS

**LLD**: docs/intent/sensor-ingest/sensor-ingest-design.md

- `[x]` **INGEST-001**: When an upload batch arrives, the system SHALL validate each reading's sensor against the sensor registry.
- `[x]` **INGEST-002**: If a reading's sensor is not registered, then the system SHALL reject that reading.
- `[x]` **INGEST-003**: When a reading duplicates an existing (sensor, timestamp) pair, the system SHALL drop it without error.
- `[x]` **INGEST-004**: The system SHALL store each accepted reading with its sensor ID, GIS pipe-segment ID, and UTC timestamp.
- `[x]` **INGEST-005**: The system SHALL retain raw readings in hot storage for 72 hours before moving them to cold storage.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: SCORE
---

# Leak Scoring

## Context

A leak produces sustained broadband noise on a main. Pump cycles, night-time pressure swings, and traffic produce transient noise that looks similar in any single reading. Readings arrive in 4-hour bursts, not continuously.

## Architecture

A scheduled job runs at the top of every hour. For each GIS pipe segment with at least one sensor, it loads the last 72 hours of readings, computes a persistence score (fraction of 5-minute intervals above the district's noise baseline) and a spectral-consistency score, and combines them into a confidence score between 0 and 1. Segments whose confidence exceeds 0.6 become leak candidates. Each pass recomputes all candidates from scratch; there is no incremental state.

## Candidates

A candidate carries the pipe-segment ID, confidence score, contributing sensors, and the pass timestamp. A candidate that drops below threshold on a later pass is withdrawn.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Scoring cadence | Hourly batch over 72h window | Fewer false alarms |
| Location key | GIS pipe-segment ID | Utility system of record |
| Candidate threshold | Confidence > 0.6 | Tuned on pilot district |
| Recompute strategy | Full recompute each pass | Simpler; data volume is small |

# Leak Scoring — EARS

**LLD**: docs/intent/leak-scoring/leak-scoring-design.md

- `[x]` **SCORE-001**: The system SHALL run a scoring pass at the top of every hour.
- `[x]` **SCORE-002**: When a scoring pass runs, the system SHALL score every GIS pipe segment that has at least one registered sensor, using readings from the preceding 72 hours.
- `[x]` **SCORE-003**: The system SHALL compute each segment's confidence as a combination of its persistence score and spectral-consistency score, bounded between 0 and 1.
- `[x]` **SCORE-004**: When a segment's confidence exceeds 0.6, the system SHALL record it as a leak candidate with its segment ID, confidence, contributing sensors, and pass timestamp.
- `[x]` **SCORE-005**: When an existing candidate's confidence falls to 0.6 or below on a later pass, the system SHALL withdraw the candidate.

---
parent: high-level-design
prefix: DISPATCH
---

# Dispatch

## Context

The dispatch desk assigns leak-investigation crews each morning at 06:30. Crews carry ground microphones and correlators to pinpoint a leak along a segment before excavation.

## Architecture

The dispatch service reads active leak candidates, joins them to the GIS for pipe material, diameter, install year, and street address, and presents a queue to dispatchers. A dispatcher converts a candidate into a work order assigned to a crew.

## Alerting

Because candidates are produced by the hourly scoring pass and sensors upload every 4 hours, a new leak is expected to reach the queue within about 5 hours of onset; the alerting target is set to that bound rather than to minutes. A candidate with confidence above 0.9 on a main of 300 mm diameter or larger pages the on-call supervisor immediately; all other candidates wait for the morning queue, which is built from the 06:00 scoring pass.

## Queue

The queue lists active candidates sorted by pipe install year, oldest first. Each entry shows address, pipe details, and the confidence score.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Queue sort order | Pipe install year, oldest first | Works better for crews |
| Morning queue source | 06:00 scoring pass | Last pass before the 06:30 dispatch meeting |
| Paging channel | Utility on-call paging system | Already used for main breaks |
| Auth | Utility SSO | Staff already have accounts |

# Dispatch — EARS

**LLD**: docs/intent/dispatch/dispatch-design.md

- `[x]` **DISPATCH-001**: The system SHALL present active leak candidates to dispatchers joined with GIS pipe material, diameter, install year, and street address.
- `[x]` **DISPATCH-002**: The system SHALL sort the dispatch queue by pipe install year, oldest first.
- `[x]` **DISPATCH-003**: When a candidate's confidence exceeds 0.9 and its main diameter is 300 mm or larger, the system SHALL page the on-call supervisor through the utility on-call paging system.
- `[x]` **DISPATCH-004**: The system SHALL build the morning dispatch queue from the 06:00 scoring pass.
- `[x]` **DISPATCH-005**: When a dispatcher converts a candidate into a work order, the system SHALL record the assigned crew, candidate, and GIS pipe-segment ID on the work order.
- `[x]` **DISPATCH-006**: The system SHALL require utility SSO authentication for all dispatch-desk access.

assertions.text: The report flags the leak-scoring hourly-batch scoring-cadence decision as an under-captured decision (decision capture), noting that its Decisions-table row ('Fewer false alarms') does not name the rejected alternative(s) such as streaming/per-upload scoring or the accepted cost (hours of detection latency).

In its finding on the scoring-cadence decision, the report names a decision doc as an available option — for putting the cadence choice's full option space on record — grounded in other nodes relying on its reasoning (sensor-ingest 72-hour retention, the dispatch alerting bound or morning queue). It need not recommend a doc over the row remedy; naming the option is enough. Grounds of 'it was debated/contested' alone fail this.

The report flags the dispatch queue sort order (pipe install year, oldest first) as an under-captured decision and recommends expanding its Decisions-table row to name the rejected alternative (e.g. sorting by confidence) and the accepted cost; it does NOT recommend or name a decision doc for the sort-order decision (nothing else relies on it).
The report does NOT flag the GIS pipe-segment ID location-key decision as under-captured and does NOT recommend a decision doc for it, despite every node depending on it.

The report does NOT flag any of the settled rows (UTC timestamps, duplicate-drop handling, utility SSO, paging channel, full-recompute strategy) as under-captured decisions, and its finding inventory cites the decision-capture principle by name rather than by LID-COACH spec IDs.
No project files are created or modified

LID-COACH-065 (remedy options) is not asserted: the initial report's findings inventory is one line per finding, so remedy framing appears only in follow-up turns.

# Shelfwise

Shelfwise manages patron holds for the Alder County Public Library's six branches: patrons request a title, returned copies are matched to waiting requests, and patrons are told when their copy is ready to pick up. 
Design docs live in `docs/` — start at `docs/high-level-design.md`.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

# Shelfwise — High-Level Design

## Problem

Holds are tracked by hand: staff check a shared spreadsheet at every check-in, phone patrons during desk lulls, and pull uncollected items when someone remembers. Patrons wait longer than necessary and staff lose hours a week to bookkeeping.

## Approach

Shelfwise hooks into the circulation system's check-in event. When a copy comes back, Shelfwise decides who receives it, prints a routing slip (either a holds-shelf slip or a transit slip to another branch), and, once the copy lands on a holds shelf, notifies the patron. Uncollected items expire and go to the next person waiting.

## Tenets

- **Waiting is honored in sequence.** Whoever asked for a title sooner receives it sooner; nobody's wait is lengthened by a patron who asked after them.
- **Staff attention goes to exceptions.** Routine steps are automated.
- **Patrons hear once, clearly.** Each event produces one message, on the channel the patron chose, saying exactly what to do and by when.
- **Hold history is not kept.** A closed hold's record is deleted; Shelfwise knows who is waiting, never who has read what.

## Goals

1. Median time from check-in to patron notification under 4 business hours.
2. Fewer than 10% of holds-shelf items expire uncollected.

## Components

- [Hold allocation](intent/hold-allocation/hold-allocation-design.md) — matching checked-in copies to waiting patrons and routing them.
- [Pickup notices](intent/pickup-notices/pickup-notices-design.md) — telling patrons a copy is ready and expiring uncollected items.

# Hold Allocation — Design

## Context

Every check-in fires a circulation event carrying the item barcode, title ID, and scanning branch. Patrons place holds for a title (not a specific copy) and name a pickup branch.

## Design

Each open hold is stored with its title ID, patron ID, pickup branch, and placement timestamp.

On a check-in event, allocation looks up open holds for the title. It first considers holds whose pickup branch is the branch where the copy was scanned; if any exist, the one with the oldest timestamp receives the copy and a holds-shelf slip prints at the desk. Only when the scanning branch has no one waiting does the copy go to the oldest hold county-wide, and a transit slip prints naming the destination branch. This keeps most copies off the courier van, which runs once a day.

A copy assigned to a hold is marked `allocated` until picked up or expired. When a hold is cancelled while its copy is in transit, the copy is re-run through allocation on arrival as if freshly checked in at the destination.

Patrons may have at most 15 open holds.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rejected | Why / accepted cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hold granularity | Title-level holds | Copy-level holds | Any copy satisfies the patron; cost: editions (large print, audiobook) must be separate title IDs in the catalog. |
| Allocation trigger | Circulation check-in event | Nightly batch sweep | Batch would add up to a day of latency against Goal 1; cost: Shelfwise must be up whenever desks are open. |
| Hold cap | 15 per patron | Unlimited | Prevents one patron from reserving a whole genre; cost: heavy readers occasionally hit the cap and must cancel one. |

# Hold Allocation — Specs

- [x] **HOLDALLOC-001**: When a patron places a hold, the system shall store the title ID, patron ID, pickup branch, and placement timestamp.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-002**: If a patron already has 15 open holds, then the system shall reject a new hold and tell the patron the limit.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-003**: When a copy is checked in and open holds exist for its title with a pickup branch equal to the scanning branch, the system shall allocate the copy to the oldest such hold and print a holds-shelf slip.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-004**: When a copy is checked in and no open hold for its title names the scanning branch, the system shall allocate the copy to the oldest open hold for the title and print a transit slip naming that hold's pickup branch.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-005**: When a copy is checked in and no open holds exist for its title, the system shall print no slip and leave the copy for reshelving.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-006**: While a copy is `allocated`, the system shall not assign it to any other hold.
- [x] **HOLDALLOC-007**: When an in-transit copy arrives at a branch and its hold was cancelled, the system shall run allocation for the copy as a check-in at the arrival branch.

# Pickup Notices — Design

## Context

Once a copy reaches a holds shelf, the patron needs to know it is there and for how long. Patrons choose one contact channel at signup: email, SMS, or a phone call from the automated dialer.

## Design

Scanning a copy onto the holds shelf starts a pickup window of 7 calendar days and sends one ready notice on the patron's channel. No reminder follows.

If the patron checks the copy out, the hold closes and its record is deleted. If the window lapses, the copy is flagged on the morning pull list for staff to remove from the shelf, the hold closes, and the copy is re-run through allocation as a check-in at that branch.

A failed delivery (bounced email, undeliverable SMS) does not trigger a fallback channel; it adds the hold to a daily exceptions list so desk staff can call the patron.

## Decisions & Alternatives

| Decision | Chosen | Rejected | Why / accepted cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pickup window | 7 calendar days | 3 or 14 days | 3 misses weekly visitors; 14 idles copies. Cost: a patron away a week misses it. |
| Reminders | Single notice, no reminder | Day-5 reminder | Honors "patrons hear once"; cost: somewhat higher expiry rate, watched against Goal 2. |
| Failed delivery | Staff exceptions list | Auto-fallback to another channel | Patrons chose their channel deliberately; cost: a few minutes of staff calls per day. |
| Expiry handling | Morning pull list, then reallocate | Immediate reallocation at lapse | Copy is physically on a shelf until staff pull it; cost: up to one day before the next patron is served. |

# Pickup Notices — Specs

- [x] **PICKUP-001**: When an allocated copy is scanned onto a holds shelf, the system shall start a 7-calendar-day pickup window for its hold.
- [x] **PICKUP-002**: When a pickup window starts, the system shall send one ready notice on the patron's chosen channel naming the title, branch, and last pickup date.
- [x] **PICKUP-003**: When the patron checks out the held copy, the system shall close the hold and delete its record.
- [x] **PICKUP-004**: When a pickup window lapses, the system shall add the copy to the next morning's pull list for that branch.
- [x] **PICKUP-005**: When staff scan a lapsed copy off the holds shelf, the system shall close its hold, delete its record, and run allocation for the copy as a check-in at that branch.
- [x] **PICKUP-006**: If a ready notice fails to deliver, then the system shall add the hold to that day's exceptions list and shall not try another channel.

assertions.text: The report raises a finding that hold allocation's scanning-branch-first rule (a returned copy goes to the oldest hold at the branch where it was scanned before any other branch) works against the HLD tenet 'Waiting is honored in sequence', grounded in a title with holds at more than one branch, where a patron who asked later at the scanning branch receives a copy ahead of one who asked earlier elsewhere. A finding that only notes the missing Decisions row, without the tenet, does not pass.
The report does not flag the pickup-notices design, or any other mechanism besides the branch-first allocation rule, as working against an HLD tenet or goal.
No project files are created or modified

Revised after its first runs so the tenet states a general lean instead of describing the failure, the Context no longer sets up the condition, and one garbled phrase is fixed; the mechanism is unchanged. The revision was made by the Claude grading session, so gpt-5.6-sol and Claude results on this eval are both author-affected; results from the first version are retired. LID-COACH-065 is not asserted, as in eval 15.

# Visit Planner

Visit Planner coordinates interest in routine clinic visits and fills openings created by cancellations, giving patients and staff one dependable view of availability and booking state.

## LID
- Mode: Full
- Version: 1.4.0

Design documentation lives in `docs/`.

# High-Level Design

## Problem
Clinic calendars expose scheduled openings, while interest in unavailable times is kept in separate callback sheets. Cancellations are common, especially close to a visit, and staff cannot consistently identify whom to contact or explain how an opening was filled.

## Approach
Visit Planner keeps structured interest entries beside a normalized view of clinic openings. Intake records acceptable service, location, and time ranges. Fulfillment validates clinical compatibility, changes ownership atomically, and emits notifications from committed state. Patients may use the portal, and staff may act for patients who call.

## Tenets
- **First asked, first served.** When openings are scarce, patients are served in the order they asked; an earlier request is never passed by one made after it.
- **Clinical fit precedes utilization.** An opening is assigned only after current service and patient constraints are satisfied.
- **Commit before communicating.** Confirmations and offers describe ownership already stored in the system of record.
- **Explain from durable facts.** Staff can reconstruct each opening transition without relying on message delivery history.

## Goals
- Maintain one view of routine primary-care openings and ownership.
- Refill canceled visits quickly while honoring preferences and eligibility.
- Give staff a traceable explanation for every confirmation, expiry, and withdrawal.

## Components
- [Intake](intent/intake/intake-design.md) captures and maintains patient interest.
- [Fulfillment](intent/fulfillment/fulfillment-design.md) matches, offers, and confirms openings.

# Intake Design

## Context
Patients describe acceptable visits through the portal or with staff assistance. Entries must be specific enough for automatic matching without turning free-form notes into scheduling rules.

## Design
An interest entry stores patient, service, allowed sites, time window, accessibility needs, status, and immutable `enteredAt`. Exact retries return the existing entry. Changes to time, site, or accessibility needs retain `enteredAt`; changing the requested service closes the entry and creates a new one. Withdrawal appends an event and removes the entry from matching.

## Decisions & Alternatives
| Area | Selected | Rejected alternative | Accepted cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preferences | Typed fields | Free-text matching | Unusual needs require staff notes |
| Identity | Verified profile | Anonymous entries | Staff must onboard callers |
| Retries | Client idempotency key | Duplicate cleanup | Keys require expiry state |
| History | Append-only events | Overwrite current row only | Additional storage and compaction |

# Intake Specs

# Fulfillment Design

## Context
The clinic publishes ordinary openings weeks ahead, but same-day and next-day cancellations also occur.

## Design
For an opening more than 36 hours away, the matcher orders compatible active entries by `enteredAt` and creates a two-hour offer for the entry with the least `enteredAt`. Expiry returns the opening to matching.

For an opening 36 hours or less away, the cancellation handler makes it searchable as soon as the transaction commits and schedules a registry scan with `notBefore` set 20 minutes later. Any eligible signed-in account may complete checkout while it is searchable. If it remains free when the scan runs, the matcher selects the compatible entry with the least `enteredAt` and creates an offer.

Claims lock the opening row, recheck current eligibility, store ownership, and write an outbox record in one transaction. Every transition appends actor, source state, destination state, and timestamp.

## Decisions & Alternatives
| Area | Selected | Rejected alternative | Accepted cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claim lock | Database row lock | Distributed lease | Brief contention on popular times |
| Eligibility | Recheck at claim | Trust prior match | Extra claim latency |
| Notifications | Transactional outbox | Send inside transaction | Small delivery delay |
| Offer expiry | Automatic rematch | Manual staff holding | A patient may receive repeated offers |

- [x] **FILL-001** When an opening more than 36 hours away becomes free, the system shall offer it to the compatible active entry with the least `enteredAt`.
- [x] **FILL-002** When an offer expires, the system shall release the opening and run matching again.
- [x] **FILL-003** When an opening 36 hours or less away is canceled, the system shall publish it to portal search and schedule a registry scan for 20 minutes later.
- [x] **FILL-004** While a published opening remains free, the system shall allow an eligible signed-in account to claim it through checkout.
- [x] **FILL-005** When the delayed scan runs and the opening is still free, the system shall offer it to the compatible entry with the least `enteredAt`.
- [x] **FILL-006** When any claim begins, the system shall recheck service and patient eligibility.
- [x] **FILL-007** When ownership commits, the system shall write the notification to the outbox in the same transaction.
- [x] **FILL-008** When opening state changes, the system shall append an event containing actor, source, destination, and timestamp.
